title: Tea under glass, seven days and a half-empty hall
subtitle: In which the thrones close the visit, Hormuz is given a deadline, and Notre-Dame receives the first pope after the fire.
lede: The ceremony is over. The deadlines remain.

yesterday.title: The two thrones, the empty hall and the burning water
yesterday.teaser: Gifts among the great, overturned chairs, ships holding their breath.

body:
The chronicler opens the book on a day when the great stages still echo and the small fires do not go out. Yesterday was the twenty-fifth, the first day of this book. Today he writes the second.

I. The thrones after the dance

In Washington the two thrones had danced for three days. The American and Chinese presidents ended the state visit with tea at the White House and a walk through the National Archives, where the Constitution and the Bill of Rights lie under glass. The ceremony was lavish: flyovers, a state banquet with the lords of technology, pandas for Atlanta. Trump spoke of friendship, strength and success; Xi of a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity. The trade truce that was to expire in November was extended by two months — until 10 January. Further meetings were announced: APEC in China, the G20 in Florida. The great disputes — Taiwan, artificial intelligence, the war in Iran — remained what they were: unresolved, but wrapped in velvet. Power loves pomp when the substance is thin. 1 2

II. Seven days on the water

At the same time a new proposal lay over the burning water. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on the margins of the UN General Assembly that Tehran had sent Washington, via Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the conditions were met — lifting the naval blockade, no sanctions on Iranian oil, the release of frozen assets, a regional ceasefire including Lebanon and Yemen — the Strait of Hormuz could reopen on the sixth day and talks on a final agreement begin on the seventh. The conditions, he said, were nothing new; they already stood in the June memorandum. The White House spoke of positive and constructive talks through intermediaries. The choice, Araghchi said, now lay with the United States. 3

Yet the fire still ate at the Red Sea. The Houthis reported attacks on Aramco facilities in Yanbu and a “sensitive target” in Riyadh. Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted six ballistic missiles. France answered. President Macron said Paris would send soldiers, radar systems and air defence to Yanbu — not to join the conflict, but to protect the place through which several million barrels of oil flow each day. The route had grown more important since the Strait of Hormuz was only partly passable. So a European flag is pushed in front of a Saudi terminal while, in the background, the Mecca alliance summons its military chiefs to urgent talks. 4

III. The eastern field by day

In the eastern field the blows fell in broad daylight. Russian drones and missiles hit apartment blocks and an office building in Kyiv. Seven people died, among them a fourteen-year-old boy; dozens were wounded. Mayor Klitschko and the authorities reported the figures, which rose through the day. President Zelenskyy condemned the attacks and said that at their meeting Trump had made the final decision: Ukraine would receive licences to produce Patriot missiles. At the same time he had asked the American president to use China’s influence on Moscow to end the invasion. The licences are a hope of future defence; yesterday’s dead are already buried. 5 6

IV. The thinning hall

In the thinning hall of the United Nations another scene played out. When Benjamin Netanyahu stepped to the podium, dozens of delegations left the room. He called them moral cowards and invited the rest to leave as well if they did not wish to listen. He defended Israel’s actions, called the charge of genocide the greatest lie of the century, and claimed that many who had walked out had privately thanked Israel for striking Iran’s nuclear sites. Outside, demonstrators were arrested. The hall stayed half empty; the words echoed in the empty chairs. 7

V. The white guest

And the white guest set foot on European stone. Pope Leo XIV began his four-day journey to France. At the Élysée he urged France to remain a champion of peace and multilateralism. At UNESCO he warned that the United Nations and other multilateral bodies were living through a crisis of effectiveness; dialogue was seen as an obstacle rather than a resource, a farce rather than a chance to seek the common good. Those with power invoked the law when it served them and ignored it when it bound them. In the evening he celebrated vespers in the rebuilt Notre-Dame — the first pope to enter the cathedral since the fire of 2019. He spoke of rebirth, of heaven and earth meeting here, and of a church that must be living, diverse and near. Outside, hundreds of thousands waited. 8

The chronicler’s finding

So the twenty-fifth ended and the twenty-sixth of September began. The thrones had danced, the water still burned, the field in the east still bled, the hall was half empty, and the white guest spoke of peace in a city that had lifted its cathedral from the ash.

The chronicler closes the chapter and leaves the threads open: Will the seven-day plan be accepted? Will the Patriot licences become fact? What will the next meetings of the two thrones at APEC and the G20 bring? And whether the pope in Lourdes and Metz will find the same words he spoke in Paris. 9

Tomorrow he will read on.
